doc.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Growing up with Chicago blues and recording with Buddy Guy and Junior Wells
summary: Chicago blues of his youth, the club scene, and the session where he felt inadequate beside Buddy Guy and Junior Wells.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: How did you learn about the blues?
That’s a big blues town, isn’t it?

That’s right. It always has been. You know you talk about Chicago blues, nowadays I think it’s a misnomer. I’m not putting down the guys who are doing it now, you know, but the Chicago blues is really, when I was growing up, because that’s when people like Memphis Slim and Muddy Waters were still living there in Chicago. You know, and they had all the joints on the South Side. And I don’t use that word loosely, I mean it, “joints” you know is like what they were playing in. And they had all these great blues singers and they were recording too you know, it’s just a shame that they got recognition so late in life you know. Now it’s a big thing. Now they are superstars, they are superheroes.
Not that many of them are still here, that’s too bad.

That’s true too. B.B. King, I’m glad he’s still around. B.B. King has opened a blues place, a blues club in Los Angeles that’s doing fantastic. And he has all the guys, some of the forgotten guys, he’ll give them a booking there. And in Chicago, Buddy Guy has a club there also now you know. And most of them, they call it Chicago blues, but they’re mostly youngsters who, when I listen to them, most of them are imitating. Some are influenced. You know there is a difference between being influenced and imitating. But they are still young, and maybe because when I was growing up I heard that real gut thing, and that’s what I’m missing when I listen to them now in Chicago. I did a record date once, why they asked me to do it to be honest I don’t know, with Buddy Guy and Junior Wells. Junior Wells is the harmonica player, you know the blues player. And these guys were so earthy, so steeped in it. Because I thought I knew everything about the blues. That’s the only time in my life I ever felt inadequate playing. But it was fun though. And the record sold a lot. It’s called “Buddy and the Juniors.” It’s just been re- issued on CD also. But I stayed in the background as much as possible, because they were playing and, as they say, showing off.
